\section{The Depth Degradation Atlas}
\label{sec:atlas}

We present the Depth Degradation Atlas: a systematic empirical map of how statistical fingerprints evolve across recursive generation depths, models, and decoding strategies.
The atlas spans $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells evaluated at depths $d \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$, with depth extensions to $d{=}5$ for cross-model EDD validation (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}).

%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{In-Distribution Performance}
\label{sec:atlas:id}

Table~\ref{tab:main_matrix} reports four-class Random Forest accuracy (5-fold CV, 200 trees) across all nine cells.
Accuracy ranges from 69.6\% (Pythia, top-$k$) to 85.4\% (GPT-2~XL, temperature), all exceeding the 25\% chance baseline by a wide margin.
Two axis effects emerge.
GPT-2~XL achieves the highest accuracy under every strategy (76.6--85.4\%), followed by OLMo (74.2--82.0\%) and Pythia (69.6--78.2\%).
Top-$k$ sampling yields the lowest accuracy in every model.
The mean within-model strategy gap is 8.4~pp, comparable to the 7.1~pp mean within-strategy model gap---decoding strategy and model family contribute roughly equally to performance variance.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Four-class RF accuracy (\%) across the $3 \times 3$ atlas, with d1--d3 three-class accuracy in parentheses (chance = 25\% / 33\%). Depth-0 recall exceeds 98\% in all cells.}
\label{tab:main_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
& Nucleus & Temp.\ $\tau{=}0.9$ & Top-$k$ \\
\midrule
Pythia-1.4B  & 78.2\,(71.2) & 76.3\,(70.6) & 69.6\,(58.8) \\
OLMo-1B     & 78.8\,(75.0) & 82.0\,(76.3) & 74.2\,(66.1) \\
GPT-2~XL    & 83.3\,(79.0) & 85.4\,(82.6) & 76.6\,(69.5) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Per-class recall distribution.}
Depth-0 recall exceeds 98\% in all 9 cells, confirming that human-written text is trivially separable from any generation depth.
Among generated depths, d2 consistently yields the lowest recall (55--71\% across cells), followed by d3 (64--82\%) and d1 (70--87\%).
For example, Pythia-1.4B nucleus achieves per-class recall of d0$\,{=}\,$99\%, d1$\,{=}\,$82\%, d2$\,{=}\,$59\%, d3$\,{=}\,$76\%.
The strongest d2 recall is obtained by GPT-2~XL temperature (71\%), consistent with its highest overall accuracy.
The d2 trough reflects its position at the center of the depth gradient: d2 features overlap with both the d1 distribution above and d3 below, making it the most confusable class---consistent with the d2-vs-d3 pair being the EDD bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}).
Full per-class recall, precision, and F1 for all cells appear in Appendix~\ref{app:per_class}.

%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Feature Universality}
\label{sec:atlas:features}

Despite the 15.8~pp accuracy spread across cells, a small feature family dominates in every setting.
The 90th-percentile perplexity (\texttt{p90\_ppl}) ranks top-2 by Gini importance in all 9 cells; surprisal variance (\texttt{var\_surprisal}) in 7/9 (8/9 under SHAP; Appendix~\ref{app:permutation}).
Table~\ref{tab:feature_importance} shows the full per-cell ranking.

Cross-model feature-rank Spearman correlation averages $\bar{\rho} = 0.868$ (range $[0.619, 0.954]$): models agree on which features carry depth information even when they differ in absolute accuracy.

4	\subsection{Top-$k$ Feature Trajectories}
5	\label{app:topk_trajectories}
6	
7	Figure~\ref{fig:feature_trajectory} in the main text shows feature trajectories for nucleus ($p{=}0.95$) and temperature ($\tau{=}0.9$) sampling.
8	Top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) trajectories follow the same monotonically decreasing trend for all features but with compressed inter-depth spacing, consistent with the signal attenuation effect discussed in \S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}.
9	Concretely, the d0$\to$d1 drop in \textsc{p90\_ppl} under top-$k$ is 78\% (vs.\ 87\% for nucleus), and the d2$\to$d3 reduction is 31\% (vs.\ 39\% for nucleus).
10	Despite the magnitude reduction, feature rank ordering across depths is preserved, which explains why ordinal classifiers maintain directionality even under top-$k$ conditions.
11	
12	\subsection{Permutation Importance}
13	\label{app:permutation}
14	
15	To verify that the Gini-based importance rankings in \S\ref{sec:atlas:features} are not an artifact of the impurity measure, we compute permutation importance (5-fold CV, 10 repeats) for all 9 atlas cells.
16	The top-2 features are stable across measures: \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in 9/9 cells under both Gini and permutation importance, and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 (vs.\ 7/9 for Gini, with the additional cell being OLMo top-$k$; the single SHAP exception is GPT-2~XL top-$k$, where \textsc{p75\_ppl} displaces \textsc{var\_surprisal} to rank 3).

433	\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation.}
434	Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
435	Recursive generation depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) whose distributional properties remain close to the human source, while down-weighting or filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion under logistic regression (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments ($\Delta < 0.02$\,pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.

\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).

\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generation (LoRA fine-tuning, 1--1.5B parameter models); cross-scale experiments extend to 7--8B instruction-tuned models (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}).
This protocol isolates the recursive depth variable but diverges from wild recursive contamination, where models are pretrained on mixed corpora containing prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions; the fingerprints we identify may attenuate or shift under such diffuse exposure.
Depth signal is the dominant classification factor (5-fold CV 59--82\%, up to 2.5$\times$ chance): LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), and seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\% vs.\ 10\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
Cross-scale experiments include both instruction-tuned and base variants; the base model shows weaker but above-chance depth signal (59.9\% vs.\ 70.2\%) with non-monotonic AUC decay, suggesting instruction-tuning regularizes degradation patterns.
Real-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursive generation depths; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).
Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0); the model gap likely reflects training data composition (OLMo's Dolma includes diverse web data vs.\ Pythia/GPT-2~XL's Wikipedia/WebText).
Deployment on heterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.

\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically---as observed in all our configurations.
However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.

\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators.
For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2~XL measurements are cross-model.
Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.2\% vs.\ GPT-2~XL 85.4\%), suggesting the overlap does not confer a systematic advantage.
An ablation with OLMo-1B as reference model shows $\Delta$=4.0pp (\S2.3), suggesting moderate robustness; however, both reference models share similar scale (${\sim}$1B) and autoregressive architecture, so validation with architecturally distinct references (e.g., encoder-only or larger-scale models) remains open.
The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.

\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}; our depth features are likely susceptible.
\citet{falahati2026_curated} show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
5	Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
6	Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion under logistic regression (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments ($\Delta < 0.02$\,pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.
7	
8	\paragraph{Strategy-unknown deployment.}
9	In strategy-unknown settings, naive transfer on d1--d3 yields only 45.9\%, and d1/d2 predictions may invert.
10	A two-stage pipeline recovers 11.5\,pp over LOO, though per-model gains vary (GPT-2~XL $+$16.4\,pp vs.\ Pythia $+$8.0\,pp).
11	Practical deployment requires either strategy metadata or learned routing.
12	
13	\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
14	Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
15	Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).
16	
17	\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
18	The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled LoRA fine-tuning (1--1.5B models), isolating the depth variable but diverging from wild contamination where models train on mixed corpora with prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions.
19	Domain bias controls confirm depth as the dominant factor: LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
20	Cross-scale experiments (7--8B, \S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) show weaker but above-chance signal; a base-model control suggests instruction-tuning regularizes degradation.
21	Segment-level estimation in mixed-depth documents remains open.
22	
23	\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
24	On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).
25	Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0); the model gap likely reflects training data composition (OLMo's Dolma includes diverse web data vs.\ Pythia/GPT-2~XL's Wikipedia/WebText).
26	Deployment on heterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.
27	
28	\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
29	Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.
30	
31	\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
32	Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically, as observed in all our configurations.
33	However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
34	Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
35	In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
36	The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.
37	
38	\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
39	Reference model choice affects classification accuracy by up to 11\,pp; same-family references yield optimal performance, though all configurations exceed $2.5\times$ chance.
40	Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators.
41	For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2~XL measurements are cross-model.
42	Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.7\% vs.\ GPT-2~XL 85.9\%), suggesting the overlap does not confer a systematic advantage.
43	An ablation with OLMo-1B and GPT-2 XL as alternative references shows accuracy ranging from 67--79\% across three reference architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}), all exceeding $2.5\times$ chance; same-family reference yields optimal performance ($\Delta{\leq}$11\,pp).
44	The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.
45	Reference-free surface features alone achieve 53.7\% (confirming partial signal in lexical statistics) but 25pp below the full pipeline, underscoring that surprisal-based features are essential.
46	Simple multi-reference ensembling does not outperform the best single reference (73.7\% vs.\ 78.6\%).
47	
48	\paragraph{Single LoRA instance.}
49	Independent replication with seed=43 yields 77.15\% (95\% CI [76.4, 78.15], $\Delta{=}{-}1.05$\,pp vs.\ baseline); cross-seed transfer retains 76.76\% ($\Delta{=}{-}1.30$\,pp vs.\ within-seed avg), confirming depth signal is inherent to the recursive process rather than specific LoRA weights (Appendix~\ref{app:seed_replication}).
50	Top-5 feature importance is identical across seeds.
51	
52	\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
53	Depth signal scales with passage length (68.4\% at 128 tokens, 77.8\% at 512; Appendix~\ref{app:length_ablation}), saturating near 500 tokens.
54	Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and curated synthetic data may not trigger collapse \cite{falahati2026_curated}, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.
55	
56	\section*{Ethics Statement}
57	
58	This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
59	No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
60	Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
61	Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion under logistic regression (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments ($\Delta < 0.02$\,pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.

\paragraph{Strategy-unknown deployment.}
In strategy-unknown settings, naive transfer on d1--d3 yields only 45.9\%, and d1/d2 predictions may invert.
A two-stage pipeline recovers 11.5\,pp over LOO, though per-model gains vary (GPT-2~XL $+$16.4\,pp vs.\ Pythia $+$8.0\,pp).
Practical deployment requires either strategy metadata or learned routing.

\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).

\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled LoRA fine-tuning (1--1.5B models), isolating the depth variable but diverging from wild contamination where models train on mixed corpora with prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions.
Domain bias controls confirm depth as the dominant factor: LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
Cross-scale experiments (7--8B, \S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) show weaker but above-chance signal; a base-model control suggests instruction-tuning regularizes degradation.
Segment-level estimation in mixed-depth documents remains open.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).
Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0); the model gap likely reflects training data composition (OLMo's Dolma includes diverse web data vs.\ Pythia/GPT-2~XL's Wikipedia/WebText).
Deployment on heterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.

\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically, as observed in all our configurations.
However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.

\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
Reference model choice affects classification accuracy by up to 11\,pp; same-family references yield optimal performance, though all configurations exceed $2.5\times$ chance.
Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators.
For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2~XL measurements are cross-model.
Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.7\% vs.\ GPT-2~XL 85.9\%), suggesting the overlap does not confer a systematic advantage.
An ablation with OLMo-1B and GPT-2 XL as alternative references shows accuracy ranging from 67--79\% across three reference architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}), all exceeding $2.5\times$ chance; same-family reference yields optimal performance ($\Delta{\leq}$11\,pp).
The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.
Reference-free surface features alone achieve 53.7\% (confirming partial signal in lexical statistics) but 25pp below the full pipeline, underscoring that surprisal-based features are essential.
Simple multi-reference ensembling does not outperform the best single reference (73.7\% vs.\ 78.6\%).

\paragraph{Single LoRA instance.}
Independent replication with seed=43 yields 77.15\% (95\% CI [76.4, 78.15], $\Delta{=}{-}1.05$\,pp vs.\ baseline); cross-seed transfer retains 76.76\% ($\Delta{=}{-}1.30$\,pp vs.\ within-seed avg), confirming depth signal is inherent to the recursive process rather than specific LoRA weights (Appendix~\ref{app:seed_replication}).
Top-5 feature importance is identical across seeds.

\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
Depth signal scales with passage length (68.4\% at 128 tokens, 77.8\% at 512; Appendix~\ref{app:length_ablation}), saturating near 500 tokens.
Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and curated synthetic data may not trigger collapse \cite{falahati2026_curated}, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that perplexity tail statistics achieve 69--86\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
5	These features generalize across model families without retraining, positioning depth estimation as an early-warning signal for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature,shi2025_closer_look}; zero-shot LLMs at 30--36\% (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}) confirm the signal is inaccessible from surface text alone.
6	Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck; see Limitations for detailed analysis.
7	Depth-graduated curation complements binary detection~\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, web-scale quality filtering~\cite{penedo2024_fineweb}, and watermarking~\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} as a provenance signal~\cite{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms}; pilot results are inconclusive (Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}) and adversarial robustness remains untested.
